newsitem.title: HUNGARY: HUNGARY, POLAND COMPETITIVENESS IMPROVED - JP MORGAN.
newsitem.headline: HUNGARY, POLAND COMPETITIVENESS IMPROVED - JP MORGAN.

text.p: Competitiveness in central Europe has developed on two different paths since 1992, with the Czech Republic and Slovakia registering significant erosion but Poland and Hungary improving, JP Morgan said on Thursday.
JP Morgan analysts surveyed the relative wage and productivity performance of the "Visegrad Four" countries, looking at changes in unit labour costs in German mark terms.

Both productivity and wages increased in central Europe between 1992 and 1996 but there is a market dispersion in the size of wage gains, with the Czech Republic and Slovakia posting the strongest and Hungary the smallest, the analysts said in JP Morgan's "Data Watch: Central Europe" update.
"In DEM terms, wages in the Czech Republic more than doubled between 1992 and 1996, whereas in Hungary the rise was closer to 10 percent," they said.

Adjusting wage growth for gains in productivity, the Czech and the Slovak economies show strong increases in unit labour costs, while in Poland and especially in Hungary, productivity gains and in particular exchange rate depreciation have helped to offset wage rises, JP Morgan said.

"On a cumulative basis, there looks to be a clear gap between these two pairs of countries, with both Poland and Hungary managing to reduce the labour cost burden on manufacturers despite rising wages," the report said.

Unit labour costs in Hungary fell to about 80 percent of the 1992 level by 1996, Poland was slightly below its 1992 figure, while Slovakia posted an about 40 percent and the Czech Republic some 50 percent rise, the analysts showed on a graph.
